extracted.intended_audience: members of the congregation of St. Thomas', Islington (Victorian Anglican parishioners); general Christian citizens concerned with the 1861 census
extracted.subtask_description: A pulpit sermon addressed to parishioners connecting the national census with Christian moral duties: urging faithful completion of the census forms, right motives in civic acts, personal and family spiritual self-examination, and readiness for final judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety and uses of a national census
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerations are an obvious necessity for nations: they enable legislation for internal welfare and external defence and facilitate schemes for education and church work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preacher argues that without accurate counts 'all legislation for the internal welfare of a country and for its external defence must be mere hap-hazard work.' He notes that statistics from faithfully filled census papers aid rulers and philanthropists, and that the census should be viewed as a legitimate and useful national instrument when conducted without undue inquisitiveness and when 'The facts will be published in general abstracts only.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Fill the census paper carefully and faithfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Citizens are bound to fill the census paper carefully and faithfully and must not wilfully deceive in their returns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This duty is urged on three grounds: duty to self (public welfare affects private benefit), duty to neighbour (obligation to contribute to common good), and duty to God (obeying 'the powers that be' and avoiding robbery/deception of government). The sermon explicitly states: 'The census paper should be filled up carefully and faithfully.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Motive determines moral character of numbering
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbering people is not intrinsically sinful; it becomes wrong if done from wrong motives such as pride or ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preacher contrasts David's sinful numbering (done to gratify pride and for ambitious conquest) with a census taken 'under God, of furthering the internal welfare of the kingdom and securing the defence' which is not sinful. He stresses that 'The right thing becomes a wrong thing in us, when we do it in a wrong and sinful spirit.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Obedience to civil authority as a duty to God
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission to lawful civil ordinances (such as returning the census) is a religious duty because 'the powers that be are ordained of God.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermon cites Scripture about submitting to rulers and frames compliance with the census as consistent with Christian teaching: 'Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.' Resisting lawful authority is presented as resisting God's ordinance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat government deceitfully — it's robbery and sin
rubrics_metrics.description: Withholding truthful information or otherwise deceiving the government in census returns is morally equivalent to robbing private persons and is ungodly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preacher condemns the axiom that men may deceive government without shame: 'To rob and deceive government is no less robbery and deception, in the sight of God, than robbery and deception practised towards private persons.' This is used to support faithful returns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and industry in occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: When recording one's occupation, one should reflect whether the calling is fulfilled with industry and honesty and free from deceits and trickery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermon asks whether one's occupation is 'labouring to have a conscience void of offence towards God and towards man' and cites 'diligent in business, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord' as the Christian standard for work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masters must treat servants justly; servants must serve sincerely
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers (masters) should give to servants what is just and equal; servants should obey their masters heartily, not with mere eye-service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preacher references Scripture: 'Masters, give unto your servants that which is just and equal' and instructs servants to obey 'in singleness of heart, fearing God' and to serve 'as to the Lord.' These are moral criteria for household and workplace relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of leisure and means is a stewardship
rubrics_metrics.description: If removed from active labour by sickness or prosperity, one must account for the use of leisure and wealth as talents given by God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermon warns against living at ease and neglecting responsibilities: 'How is the leisure,—how are the means spent? Both are talents for which account must be given.' It urges faithful and godly use of time and resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family duties — spouse and children
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing the names of spouse and children on the census should prompt examination of whether marital vows have been kept and children have been trained in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preacher asks whether vows have been fulfilled: 'Have those vows been fulfilled or broken? Are they being now fulfilled? Are ye helpers or hinderers of one another’s salvation?' Regarding children: 'How have you trained them? How are you training them? Is it in the nurture and admonition of the Lord?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor and obedience to parents
rubrics_metrics.description: Young people recorded on the census should consider whether they have loved and obeyed their parents and honored them as Scripture commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermon reminds youth of the commandment with promise and warns of the 'heaviest curse' awaiting those who set light by father or mother, urging filial obedience and respect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repentance, faith, and holiness over mere profession
rubrics_metrics.description: The census omission of religion highlights that what ultimately matters is true, lived religion — repentance, faith in Christ, and holiness — not mere religious profession or denominational label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preacher notes that although the paper omits religious classification, God's 'census' divides people into foes and friends based on genuine faith: 'Did you love the Lord Jesus Christ in sincerity and truth?' He insists 'Without holiness no man shall see the Lord' and urges ensuring that the name 'Christian' is true in life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary thank-offerings are fitting but not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: Making special offerings on the census occasion is a fitting expression of thankfulness, but the Exodus half-shekel injunction was temporary and does not compel a national offering now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preacher declines a formal collection, explaining the scriptural injunction (Exod. xxx.11–16) was likely a temporary measure to fund the tabernacle. Still, he encourages voluntary thank-offerings: 'This is a very fitting season for making thank-offerings to God... You who so feel with me can act as your consciences dictate.'

rubrics_metrics.name: The census as a prompt to personal retrospection and moral accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: The questions on the census (name, age, household composition, occupation) should prompt individuals to review their past ten years: sins, mercies, troubles, and spiritual progress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermon repeatedly uses the census as a stand-point for self-examination: 'Ten years! how many sins... multitudes forgotten by me; not one unregistered in heaven. Will they appear against me? Have they been cancelled?' It counsels thanksgiving for mercies and sober accounting of failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared for the 'final census' (judgment) now
rubrics_metrics.description: One must make sure before God that one's name will be found written in the Lamb’s book of life — i.e., repent and believe now because the final judgment is coming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sermon warns that angels will enumerate the living and dead at the final judgment and that 'the choice, under God, is in our hands to-day, to-morrow may be too late.' It exhorts immediate repentance and faith, quoting 'There’s no repentance in the grave, Nor hope of pardon there.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Support public and religious works by accurate returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Accurate census returns directly facilitate public improvements (legislation, education) and the work of the Church and philanthropic agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preacher links faithful filling of forms to practical benefits: 'Not only distinctive legislation, but also all our schemes for the extension of education and the promotion of the work of Christ’s Church can only find arguments, exactitude, and adaptation from the knowledge to be gained by a national census.'
